In this Seestar S30 Plus review, I share my backyard astrophotography results and explain where it fits between the original Seestar S30 and S30 Pro.

After about a week of testing, I’ve captured the Andromeda Galaxy, Horsehead Nebula, and Sun, tried both alt-az and EQ mode, and explored the separate wide-angle camera. There’s plenty to like about this portable smart telescope, along with a few limitations to understand before buying.

The S30 Plus combines a telescope, cameras, automatic tracking, and live image stacking in one compact setup controlled from your phone. Its dual 2K cameras produce 1440 × 2560 images, offering more resolution than the original S30 while keeping the price below the S30 Pro.

In this video, I cover:

• Seestar S30 Plus vs. S30 vs. S30 Pro: what’s different?
• My deep-sky images and first impressions
• What “dual 2K imaging” actually means
• Alt-az vs. EQ mode and my preferred exposure length
• Choosing the built-in filter for galaxies and nebulae
• Wide-angle Milky Way, star-trail, and time-lapse modes
• Battery performance during cold, damp nights
• Storage, FITS files, and USB transfer quirks
• Solar imaging with the supplied solar filter
• Who should buy the S30 Plus—and whether it’s worth upgrading

Sky-Watcher HEQ5-R Pro Review!

Can a traditional equatorial mount still be a great choice for astrophotography? I’ve been using the HEQ5-R Pro in my backyard with everything from compact refractors to an 8-inch Newtonian, and this review is based on what it’s actually like to set up and image with.

I’ll show you the mount in use, talk about how it handles different telescope rigs, and share what stood out to me. The belt-driven slewing is noticeably quieter than the other Sky-Watcher EQ mounts I’ve used.

I controlled it through an EQMOD cable and ASIAIR for plate solving and imaging, without ever needing to touch the included hand controller.

I also cover the practical buying questions: its 33 lb rated payload, built-in Wi-Fi, lack of an included polar scope, and how it compares with the larger EQ6-R Pro.

If you’re choosing a mount for deep-sky astrophotography (or wondering whether a traditional EQ mount still makes sense alongside today’s strain wave mounts), I hope my experience helps.

The Wolf’s Cave Nebula is a delicate blue reflection nebula located at the tip of the dark cloud Barnard 175 in the constellation Cepheus. Ashley and I brought a compact astrophotography setup to our campsite in southern Ontario during the new moon.

In this video, I share the complete experience, from packing and assembling the portable telescope to collecting each exposure beneath the Milky Way. You will also see how stacking many faint images gradually revealed the blue nebula and the enormous cloud of cosmic dust surrounding it.
